# Volume 2 — XXIII Miss Rosalind’s Romance

!!! note "Source text"
    Passages cited on the wiki pages link into this page. Only volumes at or before
    this page's cutoff are present.

“This December Friday afternoon, I believe I will stroll over to Echo Cottage,” Nell stated.
{: #nw-v02-c23-p0000 }

“Snow appears to be on the way,” Thirza remarked with uncertainty.
{: #nw-v02-c23-p0001 }

“I will arrive prior to the arrival of the snow, and my intention is to remain the entire night. Isolde is unable to attend due to having guests, and I am certain that Miss Rosalind will expect my presence this evening. Two full weeks have elapsed since my last visit.”
{: #nw-v02-c23-p0002 }

Since that day in October, Nell had frequently visited Echo Cottage. At times, she and Isolde took the road around in their drive; at other times, their path went through the woods on foot. Nell proceeded by herself whenever Isolde was unable to accompany her. A intense, beneficial bond had formed between her and Miss Rosalind, the sort that can only occur between a woman whose heart and soul retain the vigor of youth, and a girl whose lack of experience is compensated by her intuition and imagination. Nell had finally found a genuine “kindred spirit,” whereas Nell and Isolde entered the little lady’s isolated, solitary existence of dreams carrying the healthy delight and vigor of the outside world—a world Miss Rosalind, “the world forgetting, by the world forgot,” had given up participating in long ago; to the small stone dwelling, they imparted an aura of youth and actuality. Belinda the Fourth invariably welcomed them with her broadest possible grin . . . and the smiles of Belinda were terribly broad . . . holding them dear for their own merits as well as for the sake of her cherished mistress. Never had the small stone house hosted such “high jinks” as those taking place during that lovely, lingering late autumn, a time when November appeared to repeat October, and even December imitated the summer's hazes and sunlit warmth.
{: #nw-v02-c23-p0003 }

However, on this specific day, December appeared to recall its winter duty, abruptly becoming gloomy and somber with a windless stillness that forecasted approaching snow. Even so, Nell derived great pleasure from her stroll across the vast, gray labyrinth of the beechlands; she was by herself, yet she never considered it solitary; her mind filled her trail with cheerful friends, and she engaged with them in a lively, imaginary dialogue that proved more clever and enchanting than actual conversations tend to be, since individuals in reality occasionally fall disastrously short of expectations. Within an imagined gathering of select souls, every person utters precisely what you desire her to utter, thereby granting you the opportunity to state exactly what you desire to state. Accompanied by this unseeable group, Nell made her way through the forest and reached the fir lane at the exact moment large, downy flakes started floating down gently.
{: #nw-v02-c23-p0004 }

Upon reaching the initial curve, she discovered Miss Rosalind, who was positioned beneath a large fir with wide branches. A dress of vibrant, deep red was clad upon her, while a silk shawl of shimmering gray enveloped her head and shoulders.
{: #nw-v02-c23-p0005 }

“You resemble the queen of the fir tree fairies,” Nell shouted cheerfully.
{: #nw-v02-c23-p0006 }

“I believed you would arrive this evening, Nell,” Miss Rosalind said, rushing toward her. “And my happiness is doubled, because Belinda the Fourth has gone. She was forced to return to her house until tomorrow because her mother is ill. Had you not arrived, I would have felt exceedingly solitary . . . not even my echoes and dreams could have provided sufficient fellowship. Oh, Nell, you are so lovely,” she remarked abruptly, gazing upward at the slender, tall girl whose face bore a gentle pink glow from her walk. “So lovely and so youthful! Being seventeen is truly wonderful, is it not? I am quite jealous of you,” Miss Rosalind admitted frankly.
{: #nw-v02-c23-p0007 }

“However, seventeen is all you are in your soul,” Nell said with a smile.
{: #nw-v02-c23-p0008 }

“No, I’m advanced in years . . . or more accurately in my middle years, a condition considerably more terrible,” Miss Rosalind uttered with a sigh. “On occasion I am able to feign that I am not, yet on different occasions it becomes clear to me. And I am unable to accept it the way the majority of women appear to do. My defiance remains identical to how it was upon finding my initial gray hair. Currently, Nell, cease making a face as though you were attempting to comprehend. A person of seventeen is incapable of understanding. Immediately I shall act as if I am seventeen as well, an act I am capable of performing, now that you have arrived. In your palm you invariably carry youth similar to a present. A splendid evening lies ahead for us. Starting with tea . . . what is your desire for tea? Whatever meets your approval shall be served to us. Pray conceive of something pleasant and hard to digest.”
{: #nw-v02-c23-p0009 }

Noises of revelry and amusement echoed through the small stone cottage on that evening. Between the culinary efforts, the banquet, the confectionery making, the laughter, and the "pretending," Miss Rosalind and Nell indeed behaved in a manner completely inappropriate for a forty-five-year-old unmarried woman and a solemn schoolmistress. Afterwards, once exhaustion set in, they placed themselves upon the floor mat in front of the parlor hearth, which was illuminated solely by the gentle glow of the flames and fragranced wonderfully by the uncovered rose-jar belonging to Miss Rosalind atop the mantle. Outside, the breeze had grown stronger, moaning and lamenting about the roof edges while snow struck the windowpanes with quiet thuds, resembling a multitude of storm imps knocking to be let in.
{: #nw-v02-c23-p0010 }

“Nell, having you with me brings me such joy,” Miss Rosalind remarked, taking small bites of her sweet. “Without your presence, my mood would be low . . . terribly low . . . nearly as dark as navy. Fancies and imaginings suffice perfectly well during daylight hours and under bright skies, yet they fall short of comforting us once nightfall and tempest arrive. Authentic matters are required at such times. You remain unaware of this truth, however . . . youth at seventeen is always ignorant of it. For a seventeen-year-old, fantasies ARE enough, as you believe that actualities lie in store for you down the road. Back when I was seventeen, Nell, it never occurred to me that reaching forty-five would see me transformed into a silver-haired, tiny elderly spinster possessing merely visions to occupy my existence.”
{: #nw-v02-c23-p0011 }

“However, you are no old maid,” Nell remarked, offering a smile toward the yearning, woodbrown eyes of Miss Rosalind. “Old maids are created at birth . . . they do not develop later.”
{: #nw-v02-c23-p0012 }

“With playful humor, Miss Rosalind offered a parody, stating, “A few women are old maids from birth, others attain the status of an old maid, and still others find old maidenhood forced on them.””
{: #nw-v02-c23-p0013 }

“Then you are numbered among those who have managed it,” Nell said with a laugh, “and your success is so lovely that were all old maids similar to you, I believe they would become quite fashionable.”
{: #nw-v02-c23-p0014 }

“I always prefer to execute things as thoroughly as I can,” Miss Rosalind remarked thoughtfully, “and because it was my fate to become an old maid, I resolved that I would be an exceptionally pleasant one. I am considered strange by some; however, that is merely because I pursue my personal manner of being an old maid instead of imitating the conventional model. Nell, has anybody ever mentioned a single thing to you regarding Stephen Stanhope and myself?”
{: #nw-v02-c23-p0015 }

“Yes,” Nell admitted frankly, “it has come to my attention that you and he used to be engaged.”
{: #nw-v02-c23-p0016 }

“So we were . . . a quarter of a century back . . . a whole lifetime back. And our marriage was supposed to take place the following spring. I had prepared my wedding gown, even though no one except mother and Stephen was ever aware of that. One could say we had been engaged in some manner nearly our entire lives. During Stephen's childhood, his mother used to accompany him to this place whenever she visited my mother; and on his very second visit . . . he was nine years old and I was six . . . he informed me in the garden that he was nearly certain he would marry me upon growing up. I recall replying ‘Thank you’; and after his departure, I informed mother with great seriousness that a heavy burden had been lifted from my thoughts, since I no longer feared becoming an old maid. How poor mother laughed!”
{: #nw-v02-c23-p0017 }

“And what failed?” Nell gasped out.
{: #nw-v02-c23-p0018 }

“We merely had an absurd, foolish, ordinary fight. It was so ordinary that, if you can believe it, I cannot even recall precisely what started it. I am barely sure which of us was more at fault. Stephen actually started it, though I imagine I goaded him through some folly of my own. You see, he had a couple of rivals. I was conceited and flirting, and I enjoyed teasing him slightly. He was an extremely nervous, easily hurt guy. Anyway, both of us left in an angry mood. However, I assumed everything would be resolved; and it would have been had Stephen not returned prematurely. Nell, my dear, I regret to tell you” . . . Miss Rosalind lowered her tone as though she were on the verge of admitting a desire to kill folks, “that I am an awfully moody individual. Oh, there is no need to grin, . . . it is all too factual. I do brood; and Stephen returned before my brooding was done. I refused to hear him out and I refused to pardon him; and therefore he left permanently. He possessed too much pride to return a second time. And after that I brooded because he failed to return. Perhaps I could have summoned him, yet I was unable to demean myself to act like that. My pride matched his own . . . pride together with moodiness form a terrible mixture, Nell. However, I could never feel affection for anyone else, nor did I desire to. I was certain I would prefer being an unmarried woman for ten centuries over marrying anyone who was not Stephen Stanhope. Well, it all feels like a fantasy at present, naturally. You appear so understanding, Nell . . . as understanding as only a person of seventeen can appear. Yet do not exaggerate it. I am actually a quite cheerful, satisfied small person despite my fractured heart. My heart certainly shattered, if a heart ever did, once I understood that Stephen Stanhope was never returning. Yet, Nell, a fractured heart in actual life is not nearly as terrible as it appears in novels. It resembles a decayed tooth quite a bit . . . although you will not consider that a particularly poetic comparison. It suffers fits of pain and grants you an occasional restless night, but in the intervals it allows you to take pleasure in existence and fantasies and reverberations and peanut brittle as though nothing were wrong with it. And now you appear let down. You do not consider me nearly as fascinating an individual as you considered me five minutes prior when you thought I was constantly suffering from a sorrowful remembrance courageously concealed under outward grins. That is the most awful . . . or the finest . . . aspect of actual life, Nell. It refuses to allow you to suffer. It continues attempting to render you cozy . . . and accomplishing it...even when you are resolved to be sad and poetic. Is this sweet not delicious? I have consumed much more than is healthy for me by now, but I intend to carry on recklessly.”
{: #nw-v02-c23-p0019 }

Following a brief pause, Miss Rosalind remarked suddenly,
{: #nw-v02-c23-p0020 }

“When you arrived here on that initial day, Nell, learning of Stephen’s boy startled me. Though I have been unable to bring him up to you from that moment on, I have longed to hear everything concerning him. How would you describe the boy?”
{: #nw-v02-c23-p0021 }

“Miss Rosalind, he is the sweetest, dearest child I have ever known . . . and just like you and me, he pretends things as well.”
{: #nw-v02-c23-p0022 }

“I would like to view him,” Miss Rosalind remarked in a quiet voice, seemingly addressing only herself. “I am curious whether he resembles in any way the small dream-boy residing in this place alongside me . . . my tiny dream-boy.”
{: #nw-v02-c23-p0023 }

“I’ll have Cedric come over with me one day, if you’d care to meet him,” Nell said.
{: #nw-v02-c23-p0024 }

“It would please me . . . yet not immediately. I wish to become accustomed to the idea. It could bring greater sorrow than joy . . . should his resemblance to Stephen be too strong . . . or if he failed to resemble him sufficiently. You have my permission to present him in a month.”
{: #nw-v02-c23-p0025 }

Thus, one month afterward, Nell and Cedric traversed the forest toward the dwelling made of stone, encountering Miss Rosalind upon the path. Because she was not anticipating their arrival at that moment, her face lost its color.
{: #nw-v02-c23-p0026 }

“Thus this is the son of Stephen,” she uttered softly, grasping the hand of Cedric and gazing upon him while he remained standing, handsome and youthful, clad in his elegant small fur cap and coat. “He . . . he closely resembles his father.”
{: #nw-v02-c23-p0027 }

“Everyone claims that I am a chip off the old block,” Cedric observed, feeling totally comfortable.
{: #nw-v02-c23-p0028 }

Nell, having observed the brief occurrence, let out a breath of relief. It was evident to her that Miss Rosalind and Cedric had become fond of one another, ensuring an absence of awkwardness or formality. Despite her inclination toward romance and dreams, Miss Rosalind proved to be a most practical individual, hiding her emotions away following that initial slight slip, and she amused Cedric with as much brightness and ease as though he were the child of anyone else visiting her. A delightful afternoon was shared by everyone, followed by a lavish evening meal that would have caused old Mrs. Stanhope to raise her hands in dismay, convinced that Cedric’s stomach would be permanently damaged.
{: #nw-v02-c23-p0029 }

“Pay us another visit, my boy,” said Miss Rosalind, gripping his hand as they said goodbye.
{: #nw-v02-c23-p0030 }

“If it pleases you, you are permitted to kiss me,” Cedric stated solemnly.
{: #nw-v02-c23-p0031 }

Miss Rosalind leaned down and gave him a kiss.
{: #nw-v02-c23-p0032 }

“In what way did you realize that I wished to?” she murmured.
{: #nw-v02-c23-p0033 }

“Because the way you gazed at me was identical to how my little mother looked whenever she desired to kiss me. Generally, being kissed is not something I enjoy. Boys feel that way. Miss Penrose, you are aware of this. However, I believe I quite enjoy being kissed by you. And naturally, I will visit you another time. Provided you have no objections, I think I would enjoy having you as a special friend of mine.”
{: #nw-v02-c23-p0034 }

“I . . . I believe I won't have any objection,” Miss Rosalind said. Turning around, she went inside extremely fast; however, shortly afterward, she was at the window, smiling and waving a cheerful farewell to them.
{: #nw-v02-c23-p0035 }

While they strolled among the beech trees, Cedric declared, “Miss Rosalind pleases me. Her manner of looking at me was nice, her stone dwelling is nice, and Belinda the Fourth is nice too. It would be better if Grandma Stanhope kept a Belinda the Fourth rather than a Mary Joe. It seems certain to me that Belinda the Fourth would not consider me crazy if I shared my thoughts with her. Didn’t we enjoy a magnificent tea, teacher? According to Grandma, a boy ought not to focus on his food, yet resisting it proves difficult on occasions when he feels truly ravenous. You understand, teacher. My belief is that Miss Rosalind would not force a boy to consume breakfast porridge against his preference. She would provide him with foods he enjoyed instead. Even so” . . . Cedric possessed a great sense of fairness . . . “that could prove unhealthy for him. Still, it makes a lovely treat, teacher. You understand.”
{: #nw-v02-c23-p0036 }
